summaries.summary: RNNs are the prevalent neural approach to sentence representations in NLP and perform well across language modeling, machine translation, text classification, and parsing.
LSTM and GRU are de-facto standard RNN choices because gating units address gradient problems, long-term dependencies, and work without complex optimization or careful initialization.
Stacked RNNs enhance expressiveness by feeding hidden states from each layer to the next, benefiting from increased depth and hierarchical time series.
Conventional RNN stacking limits sophisticated recurrence-based structures, while recent alternatives encourage direct layer interaction through residual, shortcut, or LSTM cell-state connections.
The paper proposes multi-layer LSTMs using cell states to control vertical information flow through soft gating, replacing conventional stacked LSTMs with little architectural modification.
The proposed Cell-aware Stacked LSTM, or CAS-LSTM, is evaluated on SNLI, MultiNLI, Quora Question Pairs, and SST and consistently outperforms typical stacked LSTMs.
The contribution is summarized as follows.
The paper describes the proposed method in § SECREF2, experimental results in § SECREF3, related work in § SECREF4, and concludes in § SECREF5.
This section gives a detailed formulation of the architectures used in experiments.
The paper defines notation for matrices, vectors, scalars, LSTM hidden and cell states, layer and time indices, element-wise multiplication, vector components, and column vectors.
The work uses one of the most common LSTM formulations: DISPLAYFORM0 DISPLAYFORM1.
The LSTM formulation defines trainable parameters, sigmoid and hyperbolic tangent activations, and assumes INLINEFORM7 where INLINEFORM8 is the INLINEFORM9-th input to the network.
Input and forget gates control information from candidate and previous cell states, while the output gate selects the cell-state portion used in the final hidden state.
Cell states are crucial for horizontal recurrence, but the formulation ignores the lower-layer cell state and reflects lower context only rudimentarily.
Cell-aware Stacked LSTM extends stacked LSTM with an additional forget gate that accepts or ignores signals from the previous layer: DISPLAYFORM0 DISPLAYFORM1.
CAS-LSTM non-bottom layers accept hidden and cell states from left and below contexts, with Fig. FIGREF1 and Fig. FIGREF8 comparing and depicting the architecture.
Considering INLINEFORM0 is beneficial because it provides unfiltered raw information and shares feature-selection responsibility with INLINEFORM8.
Using INLINEFORM0 directly connects INLINEFORM1 and INLINEFORM2, helping and stabilizing training by easing backpropagation, as Fig. FIGREF23 illustrates.
Experiments find little difference between constant and trainable INLINEFORM0, set INLINEFORM1 throughout, and find unweighted summation degrades performance and convergence.
CAS-LSTM relates to tree-structured RNNs and Tree-LSTMs, with each CAS-LSTM layer resembling a binary Tree-LSTM on fixed right-branching trees.
CAS-LSTM is analogous to MDLSTM except for INLINEFORM0 and distinct weights per column, and differs from Grid LSTMs in producing a single hidden and cell state set.
The sentence encoder projects INLINEFORM0 one-hot words, feeds INLINEFORM3 to a INLINEFORM4-layer CAS-LSTM, and computes INLINEFORM6 by max-pooling INLINEFORM7 over time.
A bidirectional CAS-LSTM concatenates forward and backward representations and max-pools them to yield INLINEFORM2, and is called Bi-CAS-LSTM in experiments.
For natural language inference experiments, the heuristic feature-extraction function proposed by BIBREF36 is used: DISPLAYFORM0.
INLINEFORM0 means vector concatenation, and INLINEFORM1 and INLINEFORM2 are applied element-wise.
The paraphrase identification experiments use the following function: DISPLAYFORM0.
The paraphrase identification function is used as in the work of BIBREF37.
For sentiment classification, the sentence representation itself is used: DISPLAYFORM0.
The extracted feature from INLINEFORM0 is fed to an MLP classifier with ReLU activation and a fully-connected softmax layer: DISPLAYFORM0.
INLINEFORM1 is the number of label classes and INLINEFORM2 is the dimension of the MLP output.
The method is evaluated on NLI, PI, and sentiment classification, with gate-value analysis, model-variant experiments, and detailed settings in the supplemental material.
For NLI and PI, the model uses a shared sentence encoder without inter-sentence interaction to focus on semantic extraction, though CAS-LSTM applicability is broader.
NLI evaluation uses SNLI and MultiNLI, which predict entailment, contradiction, or neutral and contain about 570k and 430k premise-hypothesis pairs respectively.
NLI experiments use fixed GloVe pretrained word embeddings, 300-dimensional encoder states, a 1024D MLP, dropout, and features from Eq. EQREF28.
On SNLI, the best model achieves new state-of-the-art accuracy of 87.0% with relatively fewer parameters, while MultiNLI models match state-of-the-art accuracy on matched and mismatched test sets.
PI evaluation uses Quora Question Pairs, containing over 400k question pairs annotated for whether the two sentences are paraphrases.
PI experiments use GloVe pretrained vectors, 300D encoders, 1024D MLP, 2 CAS-LSTM layers, Eq. EQREF29 aggregation, and achieve new state of the art.

Sentiment classification uses Stanford Sentiment Treebank (SST), about 12,000 binary-parsed sentences with phrase sentiment labels, using all phrases in training and sentence-level data in evaluation.
SST-2 uses 98,794/872/1,821 training/validation/test samples for binary classification, while SST-5 uses all 318,582/1,101/2,210 samples for 5-class classification.
SST models use 300D GloVe vectors, 2-layer 150D or 300D encoders, a 300D MLP, tuned embeddings, and achieve new state-of-the-art SST-2 accuracy and competitive SST-5 accuracy.
Forget gate analysis samples 1,000 random sentences from the SNLI development set and uses a 3-layer CAS-LSTM trained on SNLI to compute gate values.
All-zero vertical forget gate values would reduce the model to a plain stacked LSTM, while all-one values would prevent effective information modulation.
Histograms from the second and third layers show vertical forget gates are not ignored and are right-skewed, possibly reflecting stronger adjacent-layer interaction.
Histograms of the range of values per time step show that a vertical forget gate effectively controls information flow by retaining or discarding signals.
The distribution of INLINEFORM0 values shows vertical forget and previous output gates make fairly different decisions, demonstrating that the direct path uses overlooked signals.
Model variations on SNLI remove or replace components from the best configuration, considering plain stacked LSTMs, different INLINEFORM0, no INLINEFORM1, and peephole lower-context integration.
Variant (iv) integrates lower contexts via the following equations: DISPLAYFORM0 DISPLAYFORM1.
Peephole weights take cell states into account, with Eq. EQREF52 and EQREF55 using the lower cell state INLINEFORM1 and making INLINEFORM4 independent of INLINEFORM5.
Table TABREF36 shows cell states improve sentence modeling, INLINEFORM0 selection has little effect, INLINEFORM1 is beneficial, and the proposed context combination outperforms BIBREF20.

CAS-LSTM stacks LSTM layers using hidden and cell states from the previous layer, achieves new state-of-the-art accuracy on SNLI and Quora Question Pairs, comparable results on MultiNLI and SST, and can replace stacked LSTMs when state sizes match.
Future work will apply CAS-LSTM beyond sentence modeling to sequence labeling, sequence generation, language modeling, and aggregating diverse sequential contexts.
The authors thank Dan Edmiston for reviewing the manuscript.
